title: Human language (Guide 1:26)
hook: the Torah speaks in human language

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moreh Nevukhim, a book written for the perplexed. You named one thing that pulls you two ways. Did you keep it where you'd see it? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-five.

A parent kneels down to a four-year-old who's just asked where the sun goes at night. The parent doesn't open with orbits and the rotation of the earth. They say something like: the sun goes to sleep on the other side of the world. It isn't a lie. It's the truth, said in words a four-year-old can hold. Later, the child will learn more, and the first answer won't feel like a trick. It'll feel like a door that opened on time. A phrase from the rabbis says the Torah does something like this. Today's word is that phrase.
screen: `WHERE DOES THE SUN GO?` → `TRUE, IN WORDS A CHILD CAN HOLD.` → `A DOOR THAT OPENS ON TIME.`

segments.voice: Human language. In Hebrew, dibrah Torah kilshon b'nei adam: the Torah speaks in the language of human beings. Turn it four ways. First, where it starts. The phrase comes from the Talmud, where some rabbis use it in arguments about how to read a verse: don't squeeze a hidden lesson out of every doubled word, they say, because people talk that way. Second, what Maimonides does with it. In chapter twenty-six of the first part of the Guide, he picks the phrase up and gives it a bigger job. The Torah, he says, speaks so that everyone can understand it, including people who aren't philosophers. And people at large, he says, can only picture something as real if it's a body, something that moves, acts, lives. So the Torah describes God with words like those: God sees, speaks, comes down, is alive. Third, an example. In the story of Babel, the verse says, "And the LORD came down to see the city and the tower." To Maimonides, this isn't a report about travel. It's the Torah using human words to say that God attends to what people do. Fourth, why it matters. This one phrase lets a reader hold the text with both hands: honoring every word, and still reading the words as speech meant for people. That was the relief the Guide offered the perplexed student we met yesterday. Now look back over this week. A loan or a job, so nobody needs to ask again. Giving where neither knows the other. The path of return. You can be Moses. A world at peace. A book for the perplexed. And today, a Torah that speaks our language.
screen: `A PHRASE FROM THE TALMUD.` · `SPOKEN SO EVERYONE CAN UNDERSTAND.` · `THE LORD CAME DOWN TO SEE.` · `HOLDING THE TEXT WITH BOTH HANDS.` · then, large: `THE TORAH SPEAKS IN HUMAN LANGUAGE.`

segments.voice: Take a moment to settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a verse you know from scripture, any one at all. Maybe one about God's hand, or God's eyes, or God walking, speaking, resting. Say it to yourself slowly. Then ask: is this a figure of speech? If it is, what is it trying to say, in plain terms? Care? Power? Attention? Don't rush to an answer. Let the picture stay a picture, and let the meaning come up underneath it. The bell holds the time.
Human language. The rabbinic phrase that the Torah speaks in the language of human beings, which Maimonides uses to read the Torah's bodily words for God as speech meant for people. Today's word.
Your line: the torah speaks our language. Today, when you explain something hard to someone, notice which words you pick so the other person can hold it. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Jews who study the Guide often read its opening chapters alongside the verses they discuss, asking of each bodily word for God what it figuratively means. The phrase 'the Torah speaks in human language' is also a familiar principle in classical commentary.

fork.setup: you're reading Genesis with a student. the verse says, "the LORD came down to see the city and the tower." the student asks: did God travel? how does Maimonides read it?
options: yes, God moved from one place to another.

notes: Guide 1:26 paraphrased: the Torah speaks in human language so that all can understand; people conceive existence through bodies, so God is described with bodily and active terms. Please confirm.

Talmudic origin: the phrase appears in several places (e.g. Bava Metzia 31b, Berakhot 31b) as Rabbi Yishmael's school's reading rule about doubled verbs; kept general ('some rabbis'). Please confirm the citation.
The Genesis 11:5 example is applied to the Guide's principle by the script; Maimonides discusses 'descending' in Guide 1:10. Confirm this is fair.
Genesis 11:5 quoted as JPS 1917; please confirm exact wording.
